# Ethics: What Should Count? {#sec-ethics-what}

::: {.callout-note icon="false" title="This content was identified, synthesized, and written by humans."}
👽 Yet, the idea that super-intelligent beings can fundamentally change the nature of science was well-prophesied in a science fiction story published in *Nature* in 2000[@chiang2000crumbs].
:::

In November 2026, Stanford psychologist Michael C. Frank made a remarkable announcement on Bluesky: he had used Claude[@anthropic2026claude] to audit 79 journal papers he had co-authored in the past five years, finding errors in more than half of his papers with shared code and data[@frank2026audit]. As described by a commentator, one reason this announcement was remarkable was because Frank helped advance the reform that makes the detection of such errors possible in the first place: open science[@osc2015reproducibility; @hardwicke2018cognition; @frank2025experimentology]. Another reason the announcement was remarkable was because it included an audit of work co-authored with the course instructor. This audit revealed that three columns of potentially sensitive data had been inadvertently uploaded to the repository, a mistake that was easy to correct but whose lessons feel difficult to ignore. Like Frank, the course instructor had dedicated their career to advocating for improvements in the quality of science — even once placing a \$3,000 error detection bounty on their own research[@coles2020redteam]. Yet, errors remain, and were discovered *in the middle of* Week 12 of the Fall 2026 *Collective \[Artificial\] Intelligence in Science* seminar (@fig-week-12-summary).

```{r}

#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-align: center
week_summary_plot(week = 12, fig_width = 12, fig_height = 5.5)
```

Ironically, this week’s seminar was initially centered on a paper published by Frank that is guaranteed to have none of the aforementioned computational or data upload errors (@fig-week-12-error-audit): a commentary proposing that scientists be evaluated by a select number of their best publications[@frank2019nbest]. This paper was assigned to prompt reflection on what academics should be prioritizing in the age of AI. For example, in addition to an emphasis on quality over quantity, one group of seminar participants described the prioritization of curiosity-related values[@poli2024curiosity]. Many researchers are drawn to science by curiosity, but this desire can quickly be overpowered by demands to get more grants, have more impact, and "publish or perish". Another group described the importance of more deeply reflecting upon our evolving roles as educators. AI is often just as quick at providing an answer as human instructors. Yet, students who rely on AI when practicing math later perform worse when tested without AI[@bastani2025guardrails], contributing to frequently-cited concerns that AI will atrophy instead of expand intellectual capabilities[@so2026collision]. Human instructors may thus have a niche teaching responsible use of AI, independent thinking skills, and a sense of personal meaning in ones educational pursuits. One does not need education for AI to provide answers. They do, however, perhaps need education to ensure that the answers AI provides are accurate, understood, and worth asking in the first place.

## Areas of consensus — and dissensus

Even before the age of AI, people did not agree about what should be valued and prioritized in science. Fortunately, identifying areas of consensus and dissensus in a collaborative setting was one of the primary goals of the course!

There was consensus agreement with Frank’s proposal: evaluate scientists based on the best work, not the sheer number of papers or citations they produce[@frank2019nbest]. There was also consensus that academic researchers need better incentives for building the infrastructure that better enables AI-driven discovery. Many of the most impressive accomplishments in AI-driven science (e.g., AlphaFold) have occurred in domains with strong data infrastructure and well-coordinated research communities[@jumper2021alphafold; @channing2026social]. Some researchers, thus, frame AI for science as a “collective social project”[@channing2026social], requiring community, coordination, cross-disciplinary education, shared benchmarks, and accessible infrastructure. This emphasis on the importance of collaboration felt particularly poignant as we approached the end of our very own collaborative effort to create this guide.

Of course, collaboration often involves navigating disagreements[@Coles2024; @dalkey1963delphi]. In a world where researchers increasingly rely on AI to find papers, seminar participants disagreed about the appropriateness of optimizing research outputs for AI discovery, consumption, and use. We also disagreed about the extent to which scientists should be rewarded for pursuing curiosity for the sake of curiosity (as opposed to more papers, grant proposals, or institutional initiatives). This, of course, is a rather fundamental disagreement about how academics should spend their time — disagreements we now understood explicitly as we entered the final week of the Fall 2026 *Collective \[Artificial\] Intelligence in Science* seminar (@sec-epilogue).
